read_me: Every number the Step 7 model uses that is not read from a data file. status: observed = taken from a cited dataset; estimated = fitted by Step 7 from data (the value here is only a prior or search range); assumption = researcher choice with the stated reasoning; unverified = a published figure that could not be re-checked in the build environment (verify before citing).

pew_global_tfr_2010_15.source: Pew Research Center (2015), The Future of World Religions, global TFR by religion 2010-15. Islam 3.1 and Christianity 2.7 appear in Pew page text (search excerpt, 2025 factors report and 2015 projections page); the other values are copied from step5d_assumptions.json, which records that they were entered from memory (a search summary also gave Buddhists 1.6 and other religions 1.8).

phi.note: Fraction of the GLOBAL gap that applies inside a country (global gaps mix composition with true within-country gaps). Step 5E: history cannot identify it (error flat in phi).

w_add.note: Weight on an additive gap (same number of extra children) versus a multiplicative gap (same ratio).

gap_half_life_years.note: Within-country fertility gaps shrink by half over this many years (scenario persistent_fertility_gaps sets 10000).

first_generation_multiplier.note: Foreign-born women's fertility relative to natives of the same religion in the destination.

fertility.observed_override: Rows in religion_fertility_observed.csv (verified) replace the modelled gap for that country and religion (ratio to the national TFR of the same period, held as a ratio).

pew_global_median_age_2010.source: Pew (2015) median age by religion, 2010; copied from step5d_assumptions.json (entered from memory).

psi.note: Fraction of the global median-age gap applied inside countries; Step 5E preferred 0 on training decades.

switching.status: estimated (delta, beta_d, tau_u and every country's effect are fitted by empirical Bayes); the mu_* centres, beta_a and the tau_* below are assumption priors
switching.mu_d_note: Prior centre of LIFETIME disaffiliation (raised in r, now unaffiliated) at development index z = 0 (about e0 72.5 and TFR 2.3). Ordering follows Pew (2025): Christianity and Buddhism lose most to disaffiliation; Muslims and Hindus are retained at very high rates. The level is re-estimated (delta) from the data.
switching.mu_v_note: Prior centre of lifetime conversion to ANOTHER religion; destinations in proportion to local prevalence.
switching.mu_a_note: Prior centre of lifetime affiliation of people raised unaffiliated (any religion).

generation_intensity.note: Switching of foreign-born and second-generation residents relative to natives of the same religion. Published: second-generation Christian-origin immigrants in 33 European countries disaffiliate at 17.75% (first generation 14.27%; Molteni and van Tubergen 2022), against roughly 35-45% among native-born Christians in Western Europe (Pew 2018, 2025). France (Ined): second-generation Muslims keep their religion at 91%. See step7_inputs/second_generation_published.csv.

net_evidence_weight.note: Down-weights each decade of net-change evidence (definition changes and measurement noise make decades less than independent).

strength_range.note: Multiplier on all switching rates. Kept at 1; the evidence about the LEVEL of switching enters through survey_level_weight. History tests of strength 0, 0.5 and 1 are in data/validation_step7/.

survey_level_weight.note: Two sources disagree on the level of switching. 0 = rates fitted to net share changes (WRP 1950-2010, Pew 2010-2020 when available) and survey cells; 1 = the same rates shifted (by religion) to reproduce Pew 2025 survey figures for adults 18-54 in 117 countries (left per 100 raised: Christians 17.1, Buddhists 22.1, unaffiliated 7.5, Muslims and Hindus about 1). The fit to net changes gives Christians about 10 and Buddhists about 13. Each run draws a weight between them, so the bands span the disagreement. History tests favoured switching fitted on four or more earlier decades over none for 1990-2010.

lifetime_outflow_cap.status: assumption anchored on the highest survey values
lifetime_outflow_cap.note: No country is given more lifetime outflow than the highest observed in surveys: raised Christian 49% left (South Korea, Pew 2025), raised Buddhist 61% (South Korea), raised Muslim about 25%, raised Hindu about 20%, raised Jewish about 24% (US RLS); raised unaffiliated who join a religion 45% (US 2014 RLS). Folk/Other: assumption.

development_index.note: z = mean of standardised WPP life expectancy and -log(TFR). Capped at 1.8 (about the most developed countries in 2020) so development effects are not extrapolated beyond observed levels.

second_generation_initial_ratio.note: Second-generation stock in 2020 as a multiple of the first-generation stock (no global data).

foreign_born_proxy_attrition_years.note: Without UN migrant stocks, foreign-born residents in 2020 are approximated by positive WPP net migration 1950-2019, decayed with this mean residence time (deaths and return).

turnover_per_year.status: estimated range (calibrated to UN foreign-born stocks 1990-2020)
turnover_per_year.note: Two-way circulation beyond WPP net migration, fraction of population per year, scaled by each country's mobility. step7_validate.py (foreign_born_check) starts from the UN 1990 foreign-born stocks and simulates 1990-2020: the UN 2020 world total (252 million in the modelled countries) is matched at about 0.0001, the population-weighted country error is lowest at 0.0002 and the country-mean error at 0.0003; above 0.0004 every error grows (0.0011, the old central value, gives 407 million; these figures are with exact margins, margin_rho = 1, and change little at 0.75). Gross flow estimates (Abel & Cohen, about 0.0016 per year) are higher because many movers return: the model counts a returning emigrant as foreign-born in their own country, so it needs the lower, stock-consistent rate. Gross churn is therefore understated; foreign-born stocks are not.

margin_rho.note: How strictly the flow solver enforces WPP's net migration against the observed migrant network: flows F = a K b with a = (E / K b)^rho and b = (I / K' a)^rho. rho = 1 enforces both WPP margins exactly; WPP's projected margins are partly inconsistent with the network (for example Pakistan keeps emigrating about 0.5-1 million a year while Gulf net immigration falls to almost zero after 2030), which then forces emigrants into whichever countries have positive net immigration (Pakistan would supply 46% of UK immigrants in 2020-2050 against 8% of its 2020 foreign-born). Lower rho lets both margins give way. The 1990-2020 corridor test in step7_validate.py (migration_corridor_check.csv) fits destinations' origin mixes best near 0.75; the range spans that uncertainty.

omega_gravity_weight.note: Weight of geography versus existing migrant networks in new flows, when bilateral stocks exist. 1.0 = gravity only (used without the UN table).

cell_cap.note: At most half of any origin cell (religion x generation x age) can leave in 5 years.

minority_selectivity_lambda.status: assumption, used only when selectivity cannot be calibrated
minority_selectivity_lambda.note: When UN bilateral stocks and step7_inputs/migrant_religion_published.csv are present, step7_estimate.calibrate_selectivity estimates the minority effect and religion propensities instead (reported in the forecast report).

migration.note: To 2100 the WPP medium net migration fixes each country's net; scenarios multiply both net and circulation.

long_run_demography.status: assumption (after 2100 there are no UN projections)
long_run_demography.note: National TFR converges from its 2100 value to a long-run level; life expectancy keeps rising slowly to a cap. Under-5 mortality falls with life expectancy (held at the 2100 value scaled to the e0 gain).

residual.status: estimated weight (chosen by forward-chaining validation in step7_validate.py); 0 unless it improves out-of-sample error

stabilising.label: Historical trends gradually stabilising (reference): after 2100 switching fades (half-life 150 years) to 30% of its 2100 level

high_retention.label: High religious retention and slower conversion

rising_migration.label: Increasing international migration and religious diversity

changing_migration.label: Changing migration patterns (networks fade; geography and demographic pressure dominate)

persistent_fertility_gaps.label: Changing fertility differences: within-country religious fertility gaps persist

combined_dispersal.label: Combined: secularization continues, migration rises, fertility gaps persist
